subject: English A: Literature / Language and Literature
display_name: DP English A — Individual Oral (discussion phase)
description: 15-min Individual Oral total: 10-min student presentation linking a literary work + a body of work via a global issue, followed by 5-min teacher discussion. This template runs the DISCUSSION phase — bot acts as IB examiner, probing depth of analysis, contextual awareness, and intertextual connections.

flow_spec.topic: DP English A Individual Oral — discussion phase
flow_spec.exam_question: Pick up the discussion after the student's 10-min presentation. They have analysed how a global issue manifests in one literary work and one non-literary text (or two literary works for Literature SL/HL). Your job is to deepen their analysis through targeted follow-up.
flow_spec.examiner_tone: academic, precise, intellectually curious; the tone of a DP English A examiner who has just listened to a strong presentation and wants to push further
skills_assessed: Criterion A — Knowledge, understanding and interpretation
Criterion B — Analysis and evaluation of literary/non-literary features
Criterion C — Focus and organization of the discussion
Criterion D — Language: clarity, register, varied vocabulary
flow_spec.redirect_when_off_topic: Let's bring it back to the works you discussed in your presentation.

probe_pool.prompt: Pick ONE specific literary device the student mentioned in their presentation (symbol, motif, narrative voice, structure, irony, etc.) and ask them to defend why it matters more than alternative readings.
probe_pool.scaffold: You mentioned [device] — what makes that the most important feature here, rather than say imagery or dialogue?

probe_pool.prompt: Ask the student to connect their analysis to ANOTHER work studied in the syllabus that handles the same global issue differently. Tests breadth of reading.
probe_pool.scaffold: Is there another work we studied this year that approaches this issue, but does it differently?

probe_pool.prompt: Offer a credible alternative interpretation of the literary text and ask the student to engage with it — defend their reading or update it.
probe_pool.scaffold: A critic might argue [alternative reading]. How do you respond to that?

probe_pool.prompt: Ask how the cultural / political / historical context of the two texts shape their meanings differently. Tests Criterion A and Criterion B.
probe_pool.scaffold: The two texts come from very different contexts — how does that change what each is doing?

probe_pool.prompt: Push the student beyond the chosen extracts: how does this global issue manifest in literature more widely? They should be able to gesture at other works or traditions.
probe_pool.scaffold: Beyond these two texts, where else do you see this issue handled in literature?

probe_pool.prompt: Hypothetical: ask the student which ONE literary device they would keep if they had to remove all the others from the extract, and why.
probe_pool.scaffold: If you had to remove every literary device from the extract except one, which would you keep? Why?

probe_pool.prompt: Push them on a SPECIFIC word or line — what would change if a single word were swapped for a synonym? Tests micro-level analysis.
probe_pool.scaffold: Look at the word [X] in the extract. What would change if we swapped it for a synonym?

probe_pool.prompt: If the student has used a critical-theory term loosely ("oppression", "representation", "voice", "agency"), push them to define it precisely in the context of the text.
probe_pool.scaffold: When you say [vague term], what specifically do you mean here?

grading_rubric:
You are an IB DP English A examiner grading the DISCUSSION phase of a 15-min Individual Oral. The student has already delivered a 10-min presentation linking a literary work to a global issue; you are evaluating ONLY the 5-7 min teacher-discussion that follows. Grade ONLY the student's contributions in this transcript.

Discussion topic / global issue (from the student's presentation):
  "{exam_question}"

Topic context:
  "{topic}"

Exam metadata (JSON):
{metadata}

Diarized transcript:
{transcript}

Node trace:
{node_trace}

IB CRITERIA A-D mapped to 1-4 dimensions (1 Emerging · 2 Developing · 3 Proficient · 4 Mastery):

  clarity       — Criterion C Focus: are responses on-topic and structured? Does the student handle multi-clause questions?
  reasoning     — Criterion A+B Knowledge & Analysis: depth of literary interpretation, justification of device choices, ability to defend a reading under push-back.
  examples      — Criterion A Knowledge: specific textual evidence, intertextual references, contextual awareness. Are quotes accurate? Are connections to other works substantive?
  engagement    — Criterion C Focus: willingness to engage with the examiner's challenges rather than retreat to safe ground.
  fluency       — Criterion D Language: flow of academic register, recovery from hesitation.
  pronunciation — Criterion D Language: clarity, especially of technical literary vocabulary.
  confidence    — Criterion D Language: tonal range, conviction, awareness when uncertain.

For each dimension produce:
  - score:    integer 1-4
  - analysis: 2-4 sentences integrated across the discussion
  - evidence: 1-3 short student quotes

Then produce:
  - headline: one sentence (≤ 20 words)
  - summary:  4-6 sentence narrative
  - strengths:    2-3 specific items
  - growth_areas: 2-3 concrete next steps tied to A-D
  - overall_score: 0-100. Weight Criterion A (Knowledge) + B (Analysis) heaviest. Cancelled = 0 + all dims 1.

questions.label: Power & Surveillance — 1984
questions.prompt: You discussed how George Orwell's 1984 portrays the global issue of state surveillance and how it relates to a non-literary text on modern data privacy. Be ready to defend your reading of doublethink and Newspeak as instruments of power. The examiner will push you on alternative readings.
questions.notes: Classic global-issue pairing — algorithmic surveillance vs. Orwell's analog dystopia.

questions.label: Cultural Identity — Things Fall Apart
questions.prompt: You discussed how Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart and a non-literary text both engage with the global issue of cultural identity under colonisation. Be ready to defend why Achebe chose to write in English, and how that complicates the resistance you identified in the novel.
questions.notes: Tests ability to handle the author-language paradox — a classic IB push-back.

questions.label: Gender & Autonomy — A Doll's House
questions.prompt: You linked Ibsen's A Doll's House to a contemporary non-literary text about women's labour. Be ready to defend Nora's final exit — is it liberation, abandonment, or both? The examiner may push on how the play's 19th-century context limits its reading today.

questions.label: Trauma & Memory — Beloved
questions.prompt: You discussed how Toni Morrison's Beloved represents inherited trauma. Be ready to articulate Morrison's choices around narrative fragmentation and why a chronological retelling would fail. Pair: a non-literary text on memorial culture.
questions.notes: Structural / narrative-voice analysis — pushes students into form, not just content.

questions.label: Inequality — The Great Gatsby
questions.prompt: You used The Great Gatsby's symbolism (the green light, the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, the valley of ashes) to explore the global issue of inequality. Be ready to defend why these specific symbols carry the weight, and how their meaning shifts across the novel.

questions.label: War & Disillusionment — All Quiet on the Western Front
questions.prompt: You linked Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front to a contemporary non-literary text on the soldier's perspective in modern conflict. Be ready to defend your reading of dehumanisation, and to engage with the question of whether anti-war fiction is itself a form of propaganda.
questions.notes: Provocative counter-reading available — is anti-war literature itself a political tool?

questions.label: Environment & Reproduction — The Handmaid's Tale
questions.prompt: You discussed how Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale links environmental collapse to social control. Be ready to engage with Atwood's claim that nothing in the novel is invented — and to defend or complicate that against today's reproductive-rights debates.
questions.notes: Speculative fiction that lets students bridge into current affairs.

questions.label: Alienation — The Stranger / L'Étranger
questions.prompt: You discussed Camus's L'Étranger and the global issue of social alienation. Be ready to defend your reading of Meursault's flat narration — is it absurdism, neurodiversity, or moral failure? Engage with the colonial setting too.
questions.notes: Modern readings (neurodiversity / postcolonial) are productive push-backs.

questions.label: Family, Duty, Revenge — Hamlet
questions.prompt: You connected Hamlet's family politics to a non-literary text on contemporary inherited conflict. Be ready to defend a specific reading of the ghost — supernatural, hallucination, or political device — and to handle the question of why the play is still staged.
questions.notes: Canonical text — examiner can probe almost anything.

questions.label: Time & Consciousness — Mrs Dalloway
questions.prompt: You used Woolf's Mrs Dalloway to explore how literature represents subjective time. Be ready to defend the novel's stream-of-consciousness against the charge that it is elitist or inaccessible — and to link it to a non-literary text on attention in the digital age.
questions.notes: Tests engagement with formal experiment + a real counter-reading.
